info.bio: El mejor grupo vocal negro de la historia del rock and roll es The Platters. Sus armonías, su estética, canciones, concepción de arreglos y disposición vocal se hicieron famosas durante una década, hasta la invasión beat. La síntesis del grupo se formó en 1952, y sus primeros discos se editaron sin éxito en una etiqueta minoritaria hasta que en 1955 fueron contratados por el sello Mercury. scenes.name: Rock'n'roll
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Fusión de rhythm'n'blues y country, con mucho más peso del primero. Chuck Berry inventa en 1955 el rock'n'roll tal como se conocerá durante cincuenta años (la guitarra como instrumento protagonista, canciones propias que hablan a los adolescentes); Bo Diddley aporta el ritmo «hambone», Little Richard y Esquerita el histerismo y el maquillaje (el primer «decadence-rock»), Jerry Lee Lewis el piano feroz y Sun Records el rockabilly. Elvis Presley es, para Scaruffi, «la primera gran estafa del rock'n'roll». Buddy Holly y Eddie Cochran abren otra vía; en paralelo nacen el soul (Ray Charles), la exótica (Martin Denny, Esquivel), la música electrónica de cinta y, en Gran Bretaña, el skiffle.

podcast.title: Male Members' Arrest (1959)
podcast.body: In 1959, all four male members of The Platters were arrested. Although initially alleged to be customers of sex workers, the charges were actually related to sharing their hotel room with white women, and all charges were later dropped. This incident negatively impacted Tony Williams' budding solo career. "not helped by all four of the male platters being arrested, allegedly as customers of sex workers, but in fact, because they were sharing their hotel room with white women."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: "Sham Corporation" Ruling (1974)
podcast.body: A court ruled in 1974 that "Five Platters Inc." was a "sham corporation" whose sole purpose was to illegally deprive band members of their ownership in the band name, and that Book Ram had unfairly benefited from an unbalanced bargaining position. This ruling briefly voided FPI's trademark. "there was a court ruling back in 1974 that the whole purpose of five platters ink had been to illegally deprive the band members of their ownership in the band name, that it was a sham corporation."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Final Name Rights Ruling (2011)
podcast.body: The complex legal disputes over The Platters' name were finally resolved in 2011. A judge ruled that Herb Reed, the last surviving member of the classic lineup (Book Ram having long died), had the rights to the name, and that "Five Platters Inc." had never owned it. "A judge finally ruled that Herb Read had the rights to the name, and that five platters ink had never owned the name."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Alex Hodge's Departure Controversy
podcast.body: Alex Hodge, an original member, left The Platters, officially due to an arrest for marijuana possession. However, Gaynell Hodge claimed that Book Ram and Herb Reed conspired to remove Alex because Alex, the alleged original founder of the group, was too knowledgeable about the music business and was becoming suspicious of Ram's financial dealings. "Gael Hodge now claims that this wasn't the real reason that Alex Hodge was sacked."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Comparison to The Ink Spots
podcast.body: The Platters were often compared to The Ink Spots, not only in their musical style, with The Platters emulating The Ink Spots in their biggest hit, but also in the unfortunate way their group eventually disintegrated due to internal conflicts and legal battles. "The platters were, in many ways, the 1950's equivalent to the ink spots."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Conflicting Legal Claims
podcast.body: In later legal cases, "Five Platters Inc." contended that band members primarily left because they were alcoholics who no longer wished to tour, and that they had willingly relinquished their rights to the band name. "five platters ink insisted that the band members had mostly left because they were alchoholics who didn't want to tour anymore, and that they'd given up their rights to the band name of their own free will."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Contrast to The Famous Flames' Style
podcast.body: The Platters represented a "smooth, sophisticated sound" in R&B, a style that The Famous Flames intentionally moved away from. The Famous Flames focused instead on "energy and for pure expression of visceral emotion." "They were going for energy and for pure expression of visceral emotion, rather than the smooth, sophisticated sounds of the Platters or Penguins."

podcast.title: Decades of Litigation
podcast.body: Following the departure of band members, 40 years of litigation ensued between Book Ram's companies and various Platters members over the rights to the band name. Court judgments were inconsistent, making it difficult to ascertain a clear legal victor from available documents. "They followed 40 years of litigation between Ram's companies and various platters members, and the judgements went both ways."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Early Formation as The Flamingos
podcast.body: The group started under the name The Flamingos, but this was a different group from the more well-known Flamingos. The initial lineup included Cornel Gunter, Gaynell Hodge, Alex Hodge, Joe Jefferson, Richard Berry, and Curtis Williams. None of the five members who sang on their biggest hits were part of this original six-person lineup. "The platters started out as the flamingos."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Early Singing Difficulties
podcast.body: Prior to their breakthrough with Mercury Records, The Platters, as signed by Book Ram, were not proficient singers. They struggled with harmony, often taking turns singing lead and failing to sing in the same key. "At the time, they didn't know how to sing in harmony. They just take turns singing lead, and often not be able to sing in the same case each other."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Film Appearance
podcast.body: They were featured in the film "Rock Around the Clock," which profoundly influenced the early perception of rock and roll in the British music business. "The idea of rock and roll in the British music business in those early years came entirely from the film Rock Around the Clock, which had featured Haley, the Platters, and Fettie Bell and his Bell Boys."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 70: "Move It" by Cliff Richard and the Drifters

podcast.title: Formation of Five Platters Inc.
podcast.body: Soon after The Platters signed with Mercury, Book Ram established a corporation named "Five Platters Inc." He controlled this entity, and all the band members were shareholders. The members assigned all rights to the band's name to this corporation, a move that would later become central to decades of legal disputes. "a corporation was set up, five platters ink, which was controlled by Book Ram, and had all the members of the platters as shareholders."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Formed from The Flamingos
podcast.body: The remaining members of The Flamingos renamed themselves The Platters after Cornell Gunter and Richard Berry departed. "Gunter and Barry left soon afterwards, and the remaining members of the band renamed themselves to the platters."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Impact of Gaynell Hodge
podcast.body: Gaynell Hodge was an indispensable figure in the 1950s LA vocal group scene, and his foundational contributions meant that without him, groups like The Platters would not have existed. "without him there would have been no platters, penguins, or Jesse Bellvin."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Proliferation of "Fake" Platters Groups
podcast.body: Over the years, more than one hundred unauthorized "fake" Platters groups, none containing original members, toured, contributing to confusion and legal battles over the band's identity. This situation was compared to the proliferation of fake Ink Spots groups. "Meanwhile, over a hundred fake platters groups, with no original members, went out on the road at various points."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Renaming to The Platters
podcast.body: The group was forced to change its name from "The Flamingos" because another group with the same name achieved a hit record. They decided on "The Platters" because disc jockeys often referred to records as "platters." "So they decided that since records were often called platters by disc juckies, they might as well call themselves that."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Retirement of Name by FPI
podcast.body: Just before the 2011 ruling, "Five Platters Inc.", then managed by Jean Bennett, announced its intention to retire the name "The Platters," although this was superseded by the court's decision granting rights to Herb Reed. "Just before that ruling, five platters ink, which was now run by Jean Bennett, announced that they were going to retire the name."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Six-Month Practice Period
podcast.body: Following their signing with Mercury Records and a six-month break after their last session with Federal, The Platters underwent intensive practice. This period transformed them into a "slick, professional group" with a polished sound, leading directly to their breakthrough success. "But they spent that six months practicing, and when they got into the studio, so record for Mercury they suddenly sounded good."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Strategic Signing to Mercury Records
podcast.body: The Platters secured a deal with Mercury Records through a strategic move by their manager, Book Ram. Ram, who also managed The Penguins (fresh off their hit "Earth Angel"), insisted that Mercury sign The Platters as a condition for signing The Penguins, thereby using The Penguins' success as leverage for his preferred group. "Ram agreed to the deal, but only on the condition that Mercury signed the platters as well."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Tony Williams Vocal Overdubs
podcast.body: After Tony Williams left The Platters in 1961, Mercury Records, convinced he was the most important member, would often take recordings by the new lineup (with Sonny Turner) and overdub new lead vocals from Williams onto them for about a year or two. "Mercury would take completed recordings by the new platters lineup and overdub new lead vocals from Williams."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Transition to Adult Market
podcast.body: Although initially marketed as a rock and roll group, The Platters quickly transitioned into the more financially rewarding adult market. This involved recording albums of popular standards, appealing to a broader audience beyond the rock and roll demographic. "But while they started off marketed as a rock and roll group, they soon transitioned into the more lucrative adult market, recording albums of standards."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Vocal Sound Transformation
podcast.body: Book Ram aimed to reshape The Platters' vocal sound, drawing inspiration from 1940s groups like The Quintones and The Modernaires who featured a four-men and one-woman lineup. This led to the recruitment of Zola Taylor, whose addition was crucial to achieving Ram's desired vocal blend. "Working with The Quintones had given Ram a taste for the particular vocal blend that comes from having four men and one woman."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Zola Taylor's Membership
podcast.body: Zola Taylor was a member of The Platters before being replaced by Sandra Doyle, who had previously joined The Teenagers. "who would later be Zola Taylor's replacement in the Platters."
